stage_3_narrative.description:
This is a colonial civil portrait of three adult male figures of Afrodescendant appearance, painted in 1599 by Andrés Sánchez Gallque. The work is titled 'Los mulatos de Esmeraldas' and is housed in the Museo de América, Madrid (on deposit from the Museo del Prado collection). The painting was sent from the Real Audiencia of Quito to Spain in 1599, commissioned by Juan del Barrio de Sepúlveda, an oidor (judge) of the Real Audiencia.

The composition presents three life-size standing figures arranged in a tripartite horizontal format, each occupying roughly one-third of the canvas width. All three are depicted in frontal or frontal-three-quarter orientation, facing the viewer directly. The figures are identified by inscriptions above their heads: 'DON PZZA'S' (left), 'DON FRAN.DE AROBE. 5 6.A' (center), and 'DÓDOMINGO. 1 6.A' (right). A heraldic cartouche with decorative scrollwork appears in the upper right, containing an inscription in Latin that references 'Filipinos Catholicos Reglishanos Indiar' and dates the work to 1599. A signature or mark 'R. SHS.GA.Q' is visible in the lower right.

Each figure holds a long spear with a dark shaft and metal point in his right hand, establishing a visual rhythm of vertical elements across the composition. The spears appear to be weapons of authority or status rather than tools of labor. All three figures wear distinctive European-influenced white ruffled collars (cuello rizado) made of linen or cotton, a fashionable element of late 16th-century dress. Beneath these collars, each wears a pearl collar (collar de perlas) composed of white elliptical plaques, likely mother-of-pearl (nácar), arranged in double rows around the neck. All three also wear circular gold earrings (aros de oro) visible in both ears.

The three figures display variations in their outer garments while maintaining a coordinated ensemble. The left figure (fig_01) wears a teal-green draped garment (manta) with brown decorative trim over a brown inner tunic (camiseta) with ornamental patterns. The center figure (fig_02) wears a tan-brown draped garment (manta) with blue decorative trim over a brown camiseta, and holds a black hat with a white plume in his left hand. The right figure (fig_03) wears an orange-yellow draped garment (manta) with decorative trim and a dark green outer layer (manta) over an orange-yellow camiseta with vertical bands. A woven or straw hat (sombrero de paja) is visible on the right side of the composition near fig_03.

The reference material clarifies that these draped outer garments are not Spanish capes but rather mantas—indigenous Andean garments—though in this case they are rendered in luxury imported fabrics (silk, fine wool, damask) rather than traditional indigenous weaving materials. This hybrid material culture reflects the specific historical context of the Esmeraldas region and the documented practice of indigenous and Afrodescendant leaders obtaining licenses to wear Spanish-style dress and carry weapons. The ornamental patterns visible on the inner tunics (camisetas) are consistent with damask weave or similar decorative textiles.

The background is minimal and neutral, rendered in pale gray-brown tones, which emphasizes the three figures as the primary subject of the portrait. The composition and presentation style—three life-size standing figures in formal dress, holding weapons, wearing jewelry and European-influenced garments—suggests a portrait of authority, status, and vassal loyalty to the Spanish Crown. The heraldic cartouche and inscriptions reinforce this reading as an official or semi-official document of colonial administration.

The painting belongs to the category of colonial civil portraiture and can be classified as a retrato de casta (caste portrait) in the sense that it documents racial and cultural mestizaje (mixing), though it is not a casta painting in the strict sense of the 18th-century casta series. Instead, it represents a specific historical moment and group: the documented mulatos (men of mixed African and European or indigenous descent) of the Esmeraldas region who negotiated their status and autonomy with the Spanish Crown in the late 16th century. The work is part of the Escuela quiteña (Quito School) tradition and exemplifies the visual representation of colonial authority, mestizaje, and the complex negotiation of status and dress codes in colonial Spanish America.

No donor figure is visible in the composition. The three standing figures are the sole subjects of the portrait. The work was commissioned by Juan del Barrio de Sepúlveda (identified in the CSV metadata as the comitente or patron), but he does not appear as a depicted figure in the painting itself.

His body is squared to the picture plane, shoulders level, and his grip on the lance is firm and assured, suggesting martial competence and physical control. The formal presentation of his body—the careful arrangement of his garments, the prominent display of jewelry (gold earrings, pearl necklace), and the deliberate positioning of his weapon—communicates self-awareness and a claim to dignified status.
